records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ אֵלָ֜יו אִ֣ישׁ אֶפְרַ֗יִם מָֽה־הַדָּבָ֤ר הַזֶּה֙ עָשִׂ֣יתָ לָּ֔נוּ לְבִלְתִּי֙ קְרֹ֣אות לָ֔נוּ כִּ֥י הָלַ֖כְתָּ לְהִלָּחֵ֣ם בְּמִדְיָ֑ן וַיְרִיב֥וּן אִתּ֖וֹ בְּחָזְקָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said to him [the] man of Ephraim, what [is] the thing the this [which] you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian? And they quarreled with him with force.
pieces: Then the men of Ephraim said to Gideon, "Why have you treated us like this? You did not call us when you went out to fight Midian!" And they argued with him sharply.

L.1: And the men of Ephraim said to him, "What [is] this thing you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they quarreled with him fiercely.

R.1: The men of the tribe of Ephraim said to Gideon, "Why did you treat us this way? Why did you not call us when you went to fight the Midianites?" And they argued angrily with him.

decisions.choice: a complaint about honor: Ephraim was left out of the start of the war
decisions.reason: Ephraim was one of the largest and proudest tribes. Gideon had called Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali (6:35) and sent for Ephraim only when the Midianites were already fleeing (7:24). The men of Ephraim felt slighted. Jephthah meets the same complaint later, with a bloodier end (12:1-6).

decisions.choice: quarreled with him fiercely: a heated, angry dispute
decisions.reason: The phrase is literally "contended with him with strength". It describes an angry argument, not a fight with weapons.

decisions.choice: the man of Ephraim: the men of the tribe as a group
decisions.reason: The singular noun is collective, as often for a tribe or town ("the man of Israel", 7:23).

decisions.choice: Gideon for "him"; the tribe of Ephraim; the Midianites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Gideon, since chapter 8 opens a new scene. Readable adds "the tribe of" and names the people rather than the land.

records.heading: Gideon answers Ephraim

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם מֶה־עָשִׂ֥יתִי עַתָּ֖ה כָּכֶ֑ם הֲל֗וֹא ט֛וֹב עֹלְל֥וֹת אֶפְרַ֖יִם מִבְצִ֥יר אֲבִיעֶֽזֶר׃
records.gloss: And he said to them, what have I done now like you? [Are] not better [the] gleanings of Ephraim than [the] grape harvest of Abiezer?
pieces: He answered them, "What have I done, compared with you? Are not the grapes Ephraim gleans better than the whole harvest of Abiezer?

L.2: And he said to them, "What have I done now compared with you? [Are] not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?

R.2: Gideon answered, "What I have done is nothing compared with what you have done. The few grapes left over for Ephraim to pick are better than the whole harvest of my own clan, Abiezer.

decisions.choice: a proverb: Ephraim's small share is worth more than Abiezer's whole victory
decisions.reason: Gleanings are the grapes left on the vine after the main harvest (Leviticus 19:10). Gideon compares Ephraim's late part in the battle to gleaning and his own clan's battle to the full harvest, and says the gleaning was better: Ephraim captured the two Midianite commanders (verse 3; 7:25).

decisions.choice: Abiezer: Gideon's own clan in the tribe of Manasseh
decisions.reason: Gideon was of the clan of Abiezer (6:11, 34), a small clan (6:15), set here against the great tribe of Ephraim.

decisions.choice: both questions are rhetorical
decisions.reason: Gideon does not want an answer. He means "I have done nothing to compare with you" and "your gleanings are better". The tone is humble and calming.

decisions.choice: questions made into statements
decisions.reason: Readable states what the rhetorical questions mean and says that Abiezer was Gideon's clan.

records.source: בְּיֶדְכֶם֩ נָתַ֨ן אֱלֹהִ֜ים אֶת־שָׂרֵ֤י מִדְיָן֙ אֶת־עֹרֵ֣ב וְאֶת־זְאֵ֔ב וּמַה־יָּכֹ֖לְתִּי עֲשׂ֣וֹת כָּכֶ֑ם אָ֗ז רָפְתָ֤ה רוּחָם֙ מֵֽעָלָ֔יו בְּדַבְּר֖וֹ הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: Into your hand has given God the commanders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, and what have I been able to do like you? Then relaxed their spirit from upon him when he spoke the word the this.
pieces: God handed the commanders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, over to you. What was I able to do compared with you?" When he said this, their anger against him cooled.

L.3: Into your hand God has given the commanders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. And what was I able to do compared with you?" Then their spirit eased toward him when he spoke this word.

R.3: God let you capture Oreb and Zeeb, the commanders of Midian. What I did is nothing next to that." When Gideon said this, they stopped being angry with him.

decisions.choice: Oreb and Zeeb: the two commanders Ephraim captured and killed
decisions.reason: Ephraim seized the fords of the Jordan, caught Oreb and Zeeb, killed them and brought their heads to Gideon (7:24-25).

decisions.choice: their spirit relaxed: their anger cooled
decisions.reason: The word for spirit can mean temper or anger (Proverbs 16:32). It "sank" or "slackened": their anger toward him died down.

decisions.choice: God gave the commanders into your hand
decisions.reason: Gideon gives the credit to God, as he did before the battle (7:15). The victory is God's, and Ephraim's share in it is God's gift.

decisions.choice: statement for the question
decisions.reason: Readable states what the rhetorical question means, as in verse 2.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֥א גִדְע֖וֹן הַיַּרְדֵּ֑נָה עֹבֵ֣ר ה֗וּא וּשְׁלֹשׁ־מֵא֤וֹת הָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתּ֔וֹ עֲיֵפִ֖ים וְרֹדְפִֽים׃
records.gloss: And came Gideon to the Jordan, passing over he and three hundred the men who [were] with him, exhausted and pursuing.
pieces: Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed it, he and the 300 men with him, exhausted but still pursuing.

L.4: And Gideon came to the Jordan, crossing over, he and the 300 men who [were] with him, exhausted and pursuing.

R.4: Gideon and his 300 men came to the Jordan River and crossed it. They were worn out, but they kept on chasing the enemy.

decisions.choice: the 300 men: the small force God chose
decisions.reason: These are the men who lapped water, whom the LORD chose so that Israel could not boast that its own strength had saved it (7:2-7).

decisions.choice: exhausted and pursuing: weary, yet still in pursuit
decisions.reason: The two words stand side by side; the second goes on in spite of the first. The weariness explains the request for bread in verse 5.

decisions.choice: the Jordan River; the enemy
decisions.reason: Readable names the Jordan as a river and says who they were chasing.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ לְאַנְשֵׁ֣י סֻכּ֔וֹת תְּנוּ־נָא֙ כִּכְּר֣וֹת לֶ֔חֶם לָעָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּרַגְלָ֑י כִּי־עֲיֵפִ֣ים הֵ֔ם וְאָנֹכִ֗י רֹדֵ֛ף אַחֲרֵ֛י זֶ֥בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֖ע מַלְכֵ֥י מִדְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: And he said to [the] men of Succoth, give please round loaves of bread to the people who [are] at my feet, for exhausted [are] they, and I [am] pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, [the] kings of Midian.
pieces: He said to the men of Succoth, "Please give some loaves of bread to the troops who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."

L.5: And he said to the men of Succoth, "Give, please, loaves of bread to the people who [are] at my feet, for they [are] exhausted, and I [am] pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."

R.5: He said to the men of the town of Succoth, "Please give my men some bread. They are worn out, and I am chasing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."

decisions.choice: Succoth: an Israelite town east of the Jordan
decisions.reason: Succoth lay in the Jordan valley in the land given to Gad (Joshua 13:27), where Jacob once built shelters (Genesis 33:17). Its people were Israelites, and Gideon asks them, as fellow Israelites, for help.

decisions.choice: the people at my feet: the men who follow me
decisions.reason: "At my feet" means "following me" or "under my command" (4:10; Exodus 11:8).

decisions.choice: the people: the troops
decisions.reason: The word for "people" often means the fighting men of a force (7:2-8).

decisions.choice: troops who follow me / my men
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "the people at my feet" means; Literal keeps the picture. Readable adds "the town of".

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ שָׂרֵ֣י סֻכּ֔וֹת הֲ֠כַף זֶ֧בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֛ע עַתָּ֖ה בְּיָדֶ֑ךָ כִּֽי־נִתֵּ֥ן לִֽצְבָאֲךָ֖ לָֽחֶם׃
records.gloss: And said [the] princes of Succoth, [is the] palm of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give to your army bread?
pieces: But the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your grip, that we should give bread to your army?"

L.6: And the princes of Succoth said, "[Is] the palm of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"

R.6: But the leaders of Succoth said, "You have not caught Zebah and Zalmunna yet. Why should we give food to your army?"

decisions.choice: is the palm of Zebah ... in your hand?: have you already captured them?
decisions.reason: The officials mock Gideon: he has not yet caught the kings, so why should they help? The "palm" may simply stand for the kings' power, or it may picture the cut-off hands that some armies of the time took from fallen enemies as a count or trophy. Either way the question means "you have not beaten them yet".

decisions.choice: the refusal: fear of Midian
decisions.reason: Succoth lay on the Midianites' line of retreat. If its officials fed Gideon's men and the kings escaped, the Midianites could take revenge on the town. They choose safety over loyalty to their own people.

decisions.choice: princes: the town's leading officials
decisions.reason: The word names men in authority, here the rulers of a town alongside its elders (verse 14).

decisions.choice: princes / officials / leaders; the question made plain
decisions.reason: The word for these officials is "princes" at Literal, "officials" at Balanced and "leaders" at Readable, as elsewhere in these books. Readable states the meaning of the mocking question.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר גִּדְע֔וֹן לָכֵ֗ן בְּתֵ֧ת יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־זֶ֥בַח וְאֶת־צַלְמֻנָּ֖ע בְּיָדִ֑י וְדַשְׁתִּי֙ אֶת־בְּשַׂרְכֶ֔ם אֶת־קוֹצֵ֥י הַמִּדְבָּ֖ר וְאֶת־הַֽבַּרְקֳנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said Gideon, therefore, when gives Yahweh Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, and I will thresh your flesh with [the] thorns of the wilderness and with the briers.
pieces: Gideon said, "Very well. When {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} hands Zebah and Zalmunna over to me, I will thresh your flesh with thorns of the wilderness and with briers."

L.7: And Gideon said, "Therefore, when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gives Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will thresh your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with the briers."

R.7: Gideon answered, "All right. When {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lets me capture Zebah and Zalmunna, I will come back and tear your skin with thorns and briers from the desert."

decisions.choice: thresh: beat or tear, as grain is threshed
decisions.reason: The verb is used for threshing grain, beating or trampling it to break it apart. Gideon threatens to punish the officials harshly, as he does in verse 16. Some take it to mean dragging thorns over them like a threshing sledge.

decisions.choice: therefore: a threat that answers their refusal
decisions.reason: The word introduces the consequence of what they have just said, often a judgment (Genesis 4:15).

decisions.choice: when the LORD gives them into my hand
decisions.reason: Gideon is sure of the victory because the LORD promised it (7:9, 14-15).

decisions.choice: I will come back and tear your skin
decisions.reason: Readable says that he will return to do this and uses plain words for the threat.

records.source: וַיַּ֤עַל מִשָּׁם֙ פְּנוּאֵ֔ל וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אֲלֵיהֶ֖ם כָּזֹ֑את וַיַּעֲנ֤וּ אוֹתוֹ֙ אַנְשֵׁ֣י פְנוּאֵ֔ל כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר עָנ֖וּ אַנְשֵׁ֥י סֻכּֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And he went up from there [to] Penuel and spoke to them like this, and answered him [the] men of Penuel just as answered [the] men of Succoth.
pieces: From there he went up to Penuel and made the same request, and the men of Penuel gave him the same answer as the men of Succoth.

L.8: And he went up from there [to] Penuel and spoke to them like this, and the men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had answered.

R.8: From there he went up to the town of Penuel and asked the people for bread. But the men of Penuel gave him the same answer the men of Succoth had given.

decisions.choice: Penuel: the place where Jacob wrestled with God
decisions.reason: Jacob named the place Peniel, "face of God", after he wrestled there (Genesis 32:31-32). It lay up the Jabbok valley, east of Succoth.

decisions.choice: made the same request / asked for bread
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "spoke to them like this" refers to: the request of verse 5.

records.source: וַיֹּ֛אמֶר גַּם־לְאַנְשֵׁ֥י פְנוּאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹ֑ר בְּשׁוּבִ֣י בְשָׁל֔וֹם אֶתֹּ֖ץ אֶת־הַמִּגְדָּ֥ל הַזֶּֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And he said also to [the] men of Penuel, saying, when I return in peace, I will tear down the tower the this.
pieces: So he said to the men of Penuel as well, "When I come back safe and sound, I will tear down this tower."

L.9: And he said also to the men of Penuel, saying, "When I return in peace, I will tear down this tower."

R.9: So he told the men of Penuel, "When I come back after I win, I will tear down this tower of yours."

decisions.choice: in peace: safely, having won
decisions.reason: The word means wholeness and well-being. Returning "in peace" from war means coming back unharmed and victorious.

decisions.choice: this tower: the town's stronghold
decisions.reason: A tower was the fortified strongpoint of a town, where its people could take refuge (9:51). The men of Penuel may have trusted it to protect them from Midian, or from Gideon.

decisions.choice: safe and sound / after I win
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "in peace" means here; Readable brings out the victory it implies.

records.source: וְזֶ֨בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֜ע בַּקַּרְקֹ֗ר וּמַחֲנֵיהֶ֤ם עִמָּם֙ כַּחֲמֵ֤שֶׁת עָשָׂר֙ אֶ֔לֶף כֹּ֚ל הַנּ֣וֹתָרִ֔ים מִכֹּ֖ל מַחֲנֵ֣ה בְנֵי־קֶ֑דֶם וְהַנֹּ֣פְלִ֔ים מֵאָ֨ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ שֹׁ֥לֵֽף חָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: And Zebah and Zalmunna [were] in Karkor, and their armies with them, about fifteen thousand, all the remaining from all [the] camp of [the] sons of [the] east, and the fallen [were] a hundred and twenty thousand man drawing sword.
pieces: Zebah and Zalmunna were at Karkor with their forces, about 15,000 men. These were all that were left of the whole army of the eastern peoples; 120,000 swordsmen had fallen.

L.10: And Zebah and Zalmunna [were] in Karkor, and their armies with them, about 15,000, all who were left of all the camp of the sons of the east; and those who fell [were] 120,000 men drawing [the] sword.

R.10: Zebah and Zalmunna were at Karkor with their army of about 15,000 men. That was all that was left of the armies from the east. Already 120,000 of their soldiers had been killed.

decisions.choice: the sons of the east: the desert peoples east of Israel
decisions.reason: The phrase names the peoples of the eastern desert who came with Midian and Amalek (6:3, 33; 7:12).

decisions.choice: thousand
decisions.reason: As at Numbers 1:46, the word for "thousand" can also name a military unit, which would make these totals smaller. It is kept as "thousand" here.

decisions.choice: men drawing the sword: armed fighting men
decisions.reason: The phrase counts soldiers (20:2, 15).

decisions.choice: the eastern peoples / the armies from the east
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the peoples rather than keep "sons of the east", which in Hebrew means members of a people.

records.heading: Zebah and Zalmunna captured

records.source: וַיַּ֣עַל גִּדְע֗וֹן דֶּ֚רֶךְ הַשְּׁכוּנֵ֣י בָֽאֳהָלִ֔ים מִקֶּ֥דֶם לְנֹ֖בַח וְיָגְבֳּהָ֑ה וַיַּךְ֙ אֶת־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֔ה וְהַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה הָ֥יָה בֶֽטַח׃
records.gloss: And went up Gideon [by the] way of the dwellers in tents from [the] east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and he struck the camp, and the camp was [in] security.
pieces: Gideon went up by the route of the tent dwellers, east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and attacked the camp while it felt secure.

L.11: And Gideon went up [by] the way of those dwelling in tents, east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and he struck the camp, and the camp was secure.

R.11: Gideon went up along the road used by people who live in tents, east of the towns of Nobah and Jogbehah. He attacked the enemy camp when they were not expecting it.

decisions.choice: the way of the tent dwellers: the desert caravan route
decisions.reason: Gideon came by the route the nomads used, out on the desert side, so the Midianites did not expect an attack from that direction.

decisions.choice: secure: off guard, feeling safe
decisions.reason: The word means safety or confidence. The Midianites, far from the battlefield, thought they were safe (as Laish was, 18:7, 27).

decisions.choice: Nobah and Jogbehah: towns in Gilead
decisions.reason: Both were towns east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:35, 42).

decisions.choice: the enemy camp; when they were not expecting it
decisions.reason: Readable says whose camp it was and what "secure" meant for the battle.

records.source: וַיָּנ֗וּסוּ זֶ֚בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֔ע וַיִּרְדֹּ֖ף אַחֲרֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּלְכֹּ֞ד אֶת־שְׁנֵ֣י׀מַלְכֵ֣י מִדְיָ֗ן אֶת־זֶ֨בַח֙ וְאֶת־צַלְמֻנָּ֔ע וְכָל־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה הֶחֱרִֽיד׃
records.gloss: And fled Zebah and Zalmunna, and he pursued after them, and he captured [the] two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and all the camp he threw into panic.
pieces: Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but he chased after them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw their whole army into panic.

L.12: And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued after them, and he captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and all the camp he threw into panic.

R.12: Zebah and Zalmunna ran away, but Gideon chased them and caught both of them, the two kings of Midian. Their whole army panicked.

decisions.choice: threw into panic: terrified and scattered
decisions.reason: The verb means to make tremble or terrify. The army was routed in fear, as at the first battle (7:21-22).

decisions.choice: the army comes before its verb
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets "all the camp" first, setting the fate of the army beside the capture of the kings.

decisions.choice: Their whole army panicked
decisions.reason: Readable makes the army the subject of a short sentence.

records.source: וַיָּ֛שָׁב גִּדְע֥וֹן בֶּן־יוֹאָ֖שׁ מִן־הַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה מִֽלְמַעֲלֵ֖ה הֶחָֽרֶס׃
records.gloss: And returned Gideon son of Joash from the battle from to [the] ascent of the Heres.
pieces: Then Gideon son of Joash came back from the battle by the Heres pass.

L.13: And Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.

R.13: After the battle, Gideon son of Joash came back by the road that goes up through the Heres pass.

decisions.choice: the ascent of Heres: a pass or slope by that name
decisions.reason: The words name the route by which Gideon came back. Heres also means "sun", so the phrase could be read "from above the sun", that is, "before sunrise" or as the sun rose, and some early translations take it as a time of day. The phrase stands where a route is expected, after "from the battle", so it is read as a place. Where the pass lay is not known.

decisions.choice: ascent / pass / the road that goes up through the pass
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "ascent", a road that climbs. Balanced and Readable say "pass", a climbing route through the hills.

records.source: וַיִּלְכָּד־נַ֛עַר מֵאַנְשֵׁ֥י סֻכּ֖וֹת וַיִּשְׁאָלֵ֑הוּ וַיִּכְתֹּ֨ב אֵלָ֜יו אֶת־שָׂרֵ֤י סֻכּוֹת֙ וְאֶת־זְקֵנֶ֔יהָ שִׁבְעִ֥ים וְשִׁבְעָ֖ה אִֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And he captured a young man from [the] men of Succoth and asked him, and he wrote down for him the princes of Succoth and its elders, seventy and seven man.
pieces: He caught a young man from Succoth and questioned him, and the young man wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.

L.14: And he captured a young man from the men of Succoth and questioned him, and he wrote down for him the princes of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.

R.14: He caught a young man from Succoth and questioned him. The young man wrote down for Gideon the names of the leaders and elders of Succoth. There were seventy-seven of them.

decisions.choice: he wrote down for him: the young man wrote for Gideon
decisions.reason: The subject changes without being named: Gideon questioned the young man, and the young man wrote the list for Gideon.

decisions.choice: a young man of the town could write
decisions.reason: The list was short, a set of names. The verse shows that writing was known well enough in Israel at the time for an ordinary young man to set down names.

decisions.choice: princes and elders: the town's officials and its council
decisions.reason: The princes are the officials who answered Gideon in verse 6; the elders are the heads of families who governed a town (Ruth 4:2).

decisions.choice: the young man; the names of
decisions.reason: Balanced names the one who wrote; Readable also says that he wrote down names.

records.source: וַיָּבֹא֙ אֶל־אַנְשֵׁ֣י סֻכּ֔וֹת וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּ֖ה זֶ֣בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֑ע אֲשֶׁר֩ חֵרַפְתֶּ֨ם אוֹתִ֜י לֵאמֹ֗ר הֲ֠כַף זֶ֣בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֤ע עַתָּה֙ בְּיָדֶ֔ךָ כִּ֥י נִתֵּ֛ן לַאֲנָשֶׁ֥יךָ הַיְּעֵפִ֖ים לָֽחֶם׃
records.gloss: And he came to [the] men of Succoth and said, look, Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, [is the] palm of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give to your men the exhausted bread?
pieces: Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Look: Zebah and Zalmunna! You taunted me about them when you said, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your grip, that we should give bread to your exhausted men?'"

L.15: And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Look, Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, '[Is] the palm of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'"

R.15: Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Look! Here are Zebah and Zalmunna. You made fun of me because of them. You said, 'You have not caught Zebah and Zalmunna yet. Why should we give food to your tired men?'"

decisions.choice: look: Gideon shows them the captured kings
decisions.reason: The word points to something present. Gideon has brought the kings with him as proof.

decisions.choice: taunted: insulted, mocked
decisions.reason: The verb means to scorn or reproach someone, as Goliath taunted Israel (1 Samuel 17:10). Gideon quotes their words of verse 6 back to them, adding that his men were exhausted.

decisions.choice: the quoted question as in verse 6
decisions.reason: Each level repeats the mocking question as it rendered it in verse 6.

records.source: וַיִּקַּח֙ אֶת־זִקְנֵ֣י הָעִ֔יר וְאֶת־קוֹצֵ֥י הַמִּדְבָּ֖ר וְאֶת־הַֽבַּרְקֳנִ֑ים וַיֹּ֣דַע בָּהֶ֔ם אֵ֖ת אַנְשֵׁ֥י סֻכּֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And he took [the] elders of the city and [the] thorns of the wilderness and the briers, and he taught with them the men of Succoth.
pieces: He took the elders of the town, and with thorns of the wilderness and briers he taught the men of Succoth a lesson.

L.16: And he took the elders of the city, and the thorns of the wilderness and the briers, and he taught the men of Succoth with them.

R.16: He took the elders of the town and punished them with thorns and briers from the desert. That is how he taught the men of Succoth a lesson.

decisions.choice: he taught: Gideon made them learn by punishment
alternatives: he threshed the men of Succoth with them
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text reads "he made known" or "he taught". Some early translations read a verb with nearly the same letters, "he threshed", the word of Gideon's threat in verse 7. The Hebrew reading is kept: it says the punishment was a lesson the town would not forget. Reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: the thorns and briers of verse 7
decisions.reason: Gideon carries out the threat he made in verse 7.

decisions.choice: city / town
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word covers any walled settlement. Literal keeps "city"; Balanced and Readable say "town", which fits a place the size of Succoth.

decisions.choice: punished them; taught a lesson
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what was done with the thorns, and both Balanced and Readable add "a lesson".

records.source: וְאֶת־מִגְדַּ֥ל פְּנוּאֵ֖ל נָתָ֑ץ וַֽיַּהֲרֹ֖ג אֶת־אַנְשֵׁ֥י הָעִֽיר׃
records.gloss: And [the] tower of Penuel he tore down, and he killed [the] men of the city.
pieces: He also tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the town.

L.17: And the tower of Penuel he tore down, and he killed the men of the city.

R.17: He also tore down the tower in Penuel, and he killed the men of that town.

decisions.choice: the tower torn down, as Gideon threatened
decisions.reason: Gideon carries out the threat of verse 9. He also kills the town's men, which he had not threatened; the text reports it without comment.

decisions.choice: the tower stands first
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts "the tower of Penuel" before its verb, setting Penuel's punishment beside Succoth's in verse 16.

decisions.choice: city / town
decisions.reason: As in verse 16.

records.source: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֶל־זֶ֨בַח֙ וְאֶל־צַלְמֻנָּ֔ע אֵיפֹה֙ הָאֲנָשִׁ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֲרַגְתֶּ֖ם בְּתָב֑וֹר וַֽיֹּאמרוּ֙כָּמ֣וֹךָ כְמוֹהֶ֔ם אֶחָ֕ד כְּתֹ֖אַר בְּנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And he said to Zebah and to Zalmunna, where [are] the men whom you killed at Tabor? And they said, like you, like them, one like [the] form of [the] sons of the king.
pieces: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "What about the men you killed at Tabor?" They replied, "They were like you, every one of them with the look of a king's son."

L.18: And he said to Zebah and to Zalmunna, "Where [are] the men whom you killed at Tabor?" And they said, "As you [are], so [were] they, each one like the form of the sons of the king."

R.18: Then he asked Zebah and Zalmunna, "What about the men you killed at Mount Tabor?" They answered, "They were men like you. Every one of them looked like a prince."

decisions.choice: where are the men?: a challenge about the men they killed
decisions.reason: The question word usually means "where?". Gideon knows the men are dead; he asks in order to make the kings admit it, and their answer describes the men. So the question means "what about the men you killed?"

decisions.choice: the men killed at Tabor
decisions.reason: The killing has not been told before. It must have happened during the years of Midianite raids (6:1-6), near Mount Tabor, where Barak gathered his army (4:6).

decisions.choice: like the form of the sons of the king: noble in bearing
decisions.reason: The kings say the men looked like princes. They mean it as praise, or perhaps flattery, but it also tells Gideon who the men were (verse 19).

decisions.choice: What about the men; Mount Tabor; a prince
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the challenge means. Readable says Tabor is a mountain and puts "a king's son" as "a prince".

records.source: וַיֹּאמַ֕ר אַחַ֥י בְּנֵֽי־אִמִּ֖י הֵ֑ם חַי־יְהוָ֗ה ל֚וּ הַחֲיִתֶ֣ם אוֹתָ֔ם לֹ֥א הָרַ֖גְתִּי אֶתְכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And he said, my brothers, [the] sons of my mother [were] they; [by the] life of Yahweh, if you had let live them, not I would kill you.
pieces: He said, "They were my brothers, my own mother's sons. As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, had you spared their lives, I would not kill you."

L.19: And he said, "My brothers, the sons of my mother, [were] they. [As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you."

R.19: Gideon said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my own mother. I swear by the living {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} that if you had spared them, I would not kill you now."

decisions.choice: sons of my mother: full brothers
decisions.reason: Where a man had more than one wife (verse 30), "my mother's sons" marks the closest brothers, born of the same mother (Genesis 43:29).

decisions.choice: as the LORD lives: an oath
decisions.reason: Gideon swears by the LORD's life that what he says is true (Ruth 3:13).

decisions.choice: Gideon kills the kings to avenge his brothers
decisions.reason: As their nearest kin, Gideon had the duty to avenge his brothers' blood (Numbers 35:19). He says that he would have spared the kings if they had spared his brothers.

decisions.choice: I swear by the living LORD; spared
decisions.reason: Readable puts the oath in plain words and says "spared" for "let live".

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ לְיֶ֣תֶר בְּכוֹר֔וֹ ק֖וּם הֲרֹ֣ג אוֹתָ֑ם וְלֹא־שָׁלַ֨ף הַנַּ֤עַר חַרְבּוֹ֙ כִּ֣י יָרֵ֔א כִּ֥י עוֹדֶ֖נּוּ נָֽעַר׃
records.gloss: And he said to Jether his firstborn, rise, kill them; and not drew the young man his sword, for he was afraid, for still he [was] a young man.
pieces: Then he said to Jether, his firstborn son, "Get up and kill them!" But the boy did not draw his sword. He was afraid, because he was still young.

L.20: And he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise, kill them." But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he [was] still a young man.

R.20: Then he told his oldest son Jether, "Get up and kill them!" But Jether was only a boy, and he was too afraid to pull out his sword.

decisions.choice: the firstborn told to kill the kings
decisions.reason: Killing a defeated enemy king was an honor for the victor's family, and dying at a boy's hand a shame for the king (verse 21). Gideon gives the honor to his eldest son.

decisions.choice: young man: a boy not yet grown
decisions.reason: The word covers ages from boyhood to young manhood. Here the reason given, that he was still young, shows that Jether was a boy.

decisions.choice: the reason first
decisions.reason: Readable joins the two reasons into one sentence and puts the boy's age first.

records.source: וַיֹּ֜אמֶר זֶ֣בַח וְצַלְמֻנָּ֗ע ק֤וּם אַתָּה֙ וּפְגַע־בָּ֔נוּ כִּ֥י כָאִ֖ישׁ גְּבוּרָת֑וֹ וַיָּ֣קָם גִּדְע֗וֹן וַֽיַּהֲרֹג֙ אֶת־זֶ֣בַח וְאֶת־צַלְמֻנָּ֔ע וַיִּקַּח֙ אֶת־הַשַּׂ֣הֲרֹנִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּצַוְּארֵ֥י גְמַלֵּיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And said Zebah and Zalmunna, rise you and fall on us, for as the man, his strength. And arose Gideon and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescents which [were] on [the] necks of their camels.
pieces: Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Get up and strike us down yourself, for as the man is, so is his strength." Gideon rose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, then took the crescent ornaments from their camels' necks.

L.21: And Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall on us, for as the man [is, so is] his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that [were] on the necks of their camels.

R.21: Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Come and kill us yourself. It takes the strength of a grown man to do this." So Gideon got up and killed them. Then he took the moon-shaped ornaments from the necks of their camels.

decisions.choice: as the man, so his strength: a grown man has a man's strength
decisions.reason: The kings use a saying. A boy might strike weakly and drag out their death; a warrior would kill them cleanly. There may also be pride in it: they ask to die at the hand of a man of rank.

decisions.choice: fall on us: attack and kill us
decisions.reason: The verb "fall on" is used for striking someone down (15:12; 1 Samuel 22:17).

decisions.choice: crescent ornaments: moon-shaped pendants
decisions.reason: The word names small crescent moons, worn by women in Isaiah 3:18 and by the kings themselves in verse 26. They were costly and may have served as charms connected with the moon.

decisions.choice: a grown man; moon-shaped ornaments
decisions.reason: Readable says what the saying means and describes the crescents.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֤וּ אִֽישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶל־גִּדְע֔וֹן מְשָׁל־בָּ֨נוּ֙ גַּם־אַתָּ֔ה גַּם־בִּנְךָ֖ גַּ֣ם בֶּן־בְּנֶ֑ךָ כִּ֥י הוֹשַׁעְתָּ֖נוּ מִיַּ֥ד מִדְיָֽן׃
records.gloss: And said [the] man of Israel to Gideon, rule over us, also you, also your son, also [the] son of your son, for you have saved us from [the] hand of Midian.
pieces: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson too, for you have saved us from the power of Midian."

L.22: And the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, both you and your son and your son's son, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian."

R.22: The Israelites said to Gideon, "Rule over us. And after you, let your son and your grandson rule. You saved us from the Midianites."

decisions.choice: rule over us, you and your son and grandson: a lasting royal house
decisions.reason: The verb is "rule", not "be king", but rule handed from father to son to grandson is kingship in all but name. Israel had no king (17:6; 21:25), and the request raises the question the rest of the book and 1 Samuel 8 return to.

decisions.choice: you have saved us: they credit Gideon
decisions.reason: The LORD had reduced Gideon's army so that Israel would not say "my own hand saved me" (7:2). The men of Israel now say just that of Gideon.

decisions.choice: the hand of Midian: Midian's power
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power or control (6:1-2).

decisions.choice: the Israelites; the Midianites
decisions.reason: Readable puts "the men of Israel" as "the Israelites", since the whole people is meant, and names the people rather than Midian's "hand".

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲלֵהֶם֙ גִּדְע֔וֹן לֹֽא־אֶמְשֹׁ֤ל אֲנִי֙ בָּכֶ֔ם וְלֹֽא־יִמְשֹׁ֥ל בְּנִ֖י בָּכֶ֑ם יְהוָ֖ה יִמְשֹׁ֥ל בָּכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And said to them Gideon, not will rule I over you, and not will rule my son over you; Yahweh will rule over you.
pieces: But Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will rule over you."

L.23: And Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will rule over you."

R.23: But Gideon answered, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you either. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is the one who will rule over you."

decisions.choice: the LORD will rule over you: the LORD is Israel's king
decisions.reason: Gideon refuses the throne because Israel already has a ruler. The same conviction stands behind Samuel's words when Israel asks for a king (1 Samuel 8:7; 12:12).

decisions.choice: I ... the LORD: the two rulers set against each other
decisions.reason: Gideon adds the pronoun "I", which Hebrew does not need, and ends with the LORD's name placed first in its clause. The contrast is between Gideon and the LORD.

decisions.choice: my son will not rule
decisions.reason: Gideon's words are soon tested: he names a son Abimelech, "my father is king" (verse 31), and that son makes himself king over Shechem (9:1-6).

decisions.choice: is the one who will rule
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the emphasis on the LORD with "is the one who".

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֜ם גִּדְע֗וֹן אֶשְׁאֲלָ֤ה מִכֶּם֙ שְׁאֵלָ֔ה וּתְנוּ־לִ֕י אִ֖ישׁ נֶ֣זֶם שְׁלָל֑וֹ כִּֽי־נִזְמֵ֤י זָהָב֙ לָהֶ֔ם כִּ֥י יִשְׁמְעֵאלִ֖ים הֵֽם׃
records.gloss: And said to them Gideon, let me ask from you a request, and give to me each [the] ring of his plunder; for rings of gold [were] to them, for Ishmaelites [were] they.
pieces: Then Gideon said to them, "I do have one request: let each of you give me a ring from his plunder." The enemy had worn gold rings, because they were Ishmaelites.

L.24: And Gideon said to them, "Let me ask a request of you: give me each [one] the ring from his plunder." For they had gold rings, because they [were] Ishmaelites.

R.24: Then Gideon said, "I want to ask you for one thing. Each of you, give me a ring from the things you took from the enemy." The enemy soldiers had worn gold rings, because they were Ishmaelites.

decisions.choice: ring: an earring or nose ring
decisions.reason: The word names a ring worn in the ear (Genesis 35:4; Exodus 32:2) or in the nose (Genesis 24:47). Here the word does not say which. Aaron made the gold calf from such rings (Exodus 32:2-4).

decisions.choice: Ishmaelites: a broad name for the desert traders
decisions.reason: The Midianites are called Ishmaelites here, as the same traders are called both in Genesis 37:25-28, 36. The name seems to cover the desert peoples who traded and wore gold.

decisions.choice: the narrator's explanation
decisions.reason: The last clauses are the narrator's, not Gideon's: they explain why the plunder held so much gold.

decisions.choice: The enemy / the enemy soldiers
decisions.reason: "They" here means the defeated enemy, not the Israelites, and Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ נָת֣וֹן נִתֵּ֑ן וַֽיִּפְרְשׂוּ֙ אֶת־הַשִּׂמְלָ֔ה וַיַּשְׁלִ֣יכוּ שָׁ֔מָּה אִ֖ישׁ נֶ֥זֶם שְׁלָלֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And they said, giving we will give; and they spread out the garment, and they threw there each [the] ring of his plunder.
pieces: "We will gladly give them," they answered. So they spread out a cloak, and each man threw onto it a ring from his plunder.

L.25: And they said, "We will surely give [them]." And they spread out the garment, and each [one] threw there the ring from his plunder.

R.25: "We will be glad to give them to you," they said. They spread out a cloak, and each man threw onto it a ring he had taken from the enemy.

decisions.choice: we will surely give: a ready, emphatic yes
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled, a Hebrew way of stressing it: they agree at once and willingly.

decisions.choice: the garment: a cloak spread on the ground
decisions.reason: The word names the large outer garment that also served as a blanket (Exodus 22:25-26). Spread out, it gathered the gold in one place.

decisions.choice: gladly; each man
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express the doubled verb with "gladly". "Each man" fits the men of the army.

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י מִשְׁקַ֞ל נִזְמֵ֤י הַזָּהָב֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔ל אֶ֥לֶף וּשְׁבַע־מֵא֖וֹת זָהָ֑ב לְ֠בַד מִן־הַשַּׂהֲרֹנִ֨ים וְהַנְּטִפ֜וֹת וּבִגְדֵ֣י הָאַרְגָּמָ֗ן שֶׁעַל֙ מַלְכֵ֣י מִדְיָ֔ן וּלְבַד֙ מִן־הָ֣עֲנָק֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּצַוְּארֵ֥י גְמַלֵּיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And was [the] weight of [the] rings of the gold which he asked one thousand and seven hundred gold, apart from the crescents and the pendants and [the] garments of the purple which [were] on [the] kings of Midian, and apart from the chains which [were] on [the] necks of their camels.
pieces: The gold rings he had asked for weighed {{units:about 42 1/2 pounds|1,700 shekels}}. That was besides the crescent ornaments, the pendants and the purple clothing worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the chains on their camels' necks.

L.26: And the weight of the gold rings that he asked for was 1,700 [shekels of] gold, apart from the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments that [were] on the kings of Midian, and apart from the chains that [were] on the necks of their camels.

R.26: The gold rings that Gideon asked for weighed {{units:about 42 1/2 pounds|1,700 shekels}}. Besides this, there were the moon-shaped ornaments, the hanging jewels and the purple robes that the kings of Midian wore, and the chains from their camels' necks.

decisions.choice: 1,700 of gold: 1,700 shekels
decisions.reason: The unit is left out, as often with weights of silver and gold (Genesis 24:22). The shekel, the standard weight, is meant: more than 40 pounds of gold, a great treasure.

decisions.choice: pendants and purple: royal finery
decisions.reason: The pendants were drop-shaped jewels (Isaiah 3:19). Purple dye was rare and costly, and purple clothing marked kings and nobles (Esther 8:15).

decisions.choice: chains: necklaces
decisions.reason: The word names chains or necklaces worn at the neck (Proverbs 1:9), here on the camels, as the crescents were (verse 21).

decisions.choice: about 42 1/2 pounds / 1,700 shekels
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight, with the shekel as the reader's alternative; Literal keeps the Hebrew and brackets "shekels".

decisions.choice: moon-shaped ornaments; hanging jewels
decisions.reason: Readable describes the jewelry in plain words.

records.source: וַיַּעַשׂ֩ אוֹת֨וֹ גִדְע֜וֹן לְאֵפ֗וֹד וַיַּצֵּ֨ג אוֹת֤וֹ בְעִירוֹ֙ בְּעָפְרָ֔ה וַיִּזְנ֧וּ כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אַחֲרָ֖יו שָׁ֑ם וַיְהִ֛י לְגִדְע֥וֹן וּלְבֵית֖וֹ לְמוֹקֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And made it Gideon into an ephod and set it in his city, in Ophrah, and prostituted themselves all Israel after it there, and it became to Gideon and to his house a snare.
pieces: Gideon made the gold into an ephod and set it up in his town, Ophrah. There all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it, and it became a trap for Gideon and his family.

L.27: And Gideon made it into an ephod and set it up in his city, in Ophrah, and all Israel prostituted themselves after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.

R.27: Gideon used the gold to make an ephod, a holy object used in worship, and he set it up in his hometown of Ophrah. All the Israelites were unfaithful to God by worshiping it there. It became a trap for Gideon and his family.

decisions.choice: an ephod: a sacred object of gold, perhaps used to seek God's answers
alternatives: a gold-covered priestly vest like the high priest's
decisions.reason: In Exodus 28:6-14 the ephod is the high priest's embroidered vest, worn with the breastpiece that held the Urim and Thummim, by which God's will was asked (Exodus 28:30). Elsewhere an ephod is an object kept at a shrine and consulted for guidance (17:5; 18:14-20; 1 Samuel 23:9-12). Gideon's ephod used more than 40 pounds of gold, too heavy to wear, so it may have been a gold-covered image or object that stood in Ophrah. The text does not say what it looked like or what Gideon meant by it; it says what it became, something Israel worshiped.

decisions.choice: prostituted themselves after it: worshiped it, unfaithful to the LORD
decisions.reason: Israel's turning to other objects of worship is pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness (2:17; Exodus 34:15-16).

decisions.choice: a snare: a trap that leads into sin
decisions.reason: The LORD warned that the gods of the land would be a snare to Israel (2:3; Exodus 23:33; 34:12). Now the snare is something Israel's own deliverer made.

decisions.choice: gold gathered from the people, made into an object of worship
decisions.reason: As Aaron made the calf from the people's gold rings (Exodus 32:2-4), Gideon makes the ephod from the rings of the plunder. He sets it up in Ophrah, the town where he had torn down Baal's altar (6:25-32).

decisions.choice: prostituted themselves / were unfaithful to God by worshiping it
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the picture of prostitution, as in Exodus 34:15-16; Balanced adds "by worshiping" to say what was done with the ephod. Readable says plainly what the picture means.

decisions.choice: a holy object used in worship; family
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the word "ephod" and says briefly what kind of thing it was, without choosing between the possible forms. Balanced and Readable say "family" for "house".

records.source: וַיִּכָּנַ֣ע מִדְיָ֗ן לִפְנֵי֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְלֹ֥א יָסְפ֖וּ לָשֵׂ֣את רֹאשָׁ֑ם וַתִּשְׁקֹ֥ט הָאָ֛רֶץ אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה בִּימֵ֥י גִדְעֽוֹן׃פ
records.gloss: And was subdued Midian before [the] sons of Israel, and not they again lifted up their head; and was quiet the land forty year in [the] days of Gideon.
pieces: So Midian was humbled before the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} and did not raise its head again, and the land had peace for forty years in the days of Gideon.

L.28: And Midian was subdued before the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, and they did not again lift up their head, and the land was quiet forty years in the days of Gideon.

R.28: So Midian was beaten by the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} and was never strong enough to threaten them again. The land had peace for forty years while Gideon lived.

decisions.choice: did not lift up their head again: never recovered their strength
decisions.reason: To lift the head is to regain pride and power (Psalm 83:3). Midian could no longer threaten Israel.

decisions.choice: the land was quiet forty years
decisions.reason: The same closing words end the stories of Othniel (3:11), Ehud (3:30) and Deborah (5:31). Forty years is the span of a generation; this is the last time the book uses the words.

decisions.choice: was subdued: brought low
decisions.reason: The verb is passive and the one used when the LORD subdued Moab and Jabin (3:30; 4:23). The victory is again the LORD's.

decisions.choice: was quiet / had peace
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "was quiet"; Balanced and Readable say "had peace", as throughout Judges.

records.source: וַיֵּ֛לֶךְ יְרֻבַּ֥עַל בֶּן־יוֹאָ֖שׁ וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב בְּבֵיתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And went Jerubbaal son of Joash and dwelt in his house.
pieces: Jerubbaal son of Joash went back and lived in his own house.

L.29: And Jerubbaal son of Joash went and dwelt in his house.

R.29: Gideon son of Joash, who was also called Jerubbaal, went back to live in his own house.

decisions.choice: Jerubbaal: Gideon's other name
decisions.reason: Gideon was given this name, "let Baal contend", after he tore down Baal's altar (6:32). The book uses both names from here on (verse 35; 9:1).

decisions.choice: went and dwelt in his house: went home to private life
decisions.reason: The phrase marks the end of the campaign: the army breaks up and its leader goes home (7:8; 1 Samuel 24:23).

decisions.choice: Gideon ... who was also called Jerubbaal
decisions.reason: Readable names Gideon so that the reader does not take Jerubbaal for someone else.

records.heading: Gideon's last years

records.source: וּלְגִדְע֗וֹן הָיוּ֙ שִׁבְעִ֣ים בָּנִ֔ים יֹצְאֵ֖י יְרֵכ֑וֹ כִּֽי־נָשִׁ֥ים רַבּ֖וֹת הָ֥יוּ לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And to Gideon were seventy sons coming out of his thigh, for many wives were to him.
pieces: Gideon had seventy sons who were his own offspring, for he had many wives.

L.30: And Gideon had seventy sons coming out of his thigh, for he had many wives.

R.30: Gideon had seventy sons of his own, because he had many wives.

decisions.choice: coming out of his thigh: his own children
decisions.reason: The "thigh" stands for a man's power to father children; the phrase means his own descendants (Genesis 46:26; Exodus 1:5).

decisions.choice: seventy sons and many wives: a household like a king's
decisions.reason: Many wives and a large family were marks of a king (Deuteronomy 17:17; 2 Samuel 5:13). The seventy sons matter in the next chapter (9:2, 5).

decisions.choice: his own offspring / of his own
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the picture means; Literal keeps it.

records.source: וּפִֽילַגְשׁוֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּשְׁכֶ֔ם יָֽלְדָה־לּ֥וֹ גַם־הִ֖יא בֵּ֑ן וַיָּ֥שֶׂם אֶת־שְׁמ֖וֹ אֲבִימֶֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And his concubine who [was] in Shechem bore to him, also she, a son, and he set his name Abimelech.
pieces: His concubine who lived in Shechem bore him a son as well, and he named him Abimelech.

L.31: And his concubine who [was] in Shechem, she also bore him a son, and he set his name [as] Abimelech.

R.31: Gideon also had a concubine (a secondary wife) who lived in Shechem. She too had a son by him, and Gideon named him Abimelech.

decisions.choice: his concubine in Shechem: a wife of lower rank living with her own family
decisions.reason: A concubine was a lawful but secondary wife, without a full wife's standing (Genesis 25:6). This one stayed in Shechem with her family, and her son later uses those ties to become king there (9:1-3).

decisions.choice: Abimelech: "my father is king"
decisions.reason: The name means "my father is king". After Gideon's words in verse 23, it is a pointed choice, and the son lives up to it (9:6).

decisions.choice: he set his name: Gideon named him
decisions.reason: The verb is masculine, so it is Gideon who named the boy. The phrase may also mean he gave him this name as an added title, but the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: concubine (a secondary wife)
decisions.reason: Readable explains "concubine" the first time it appears in a chapter.

records.source: וַיָּ֛מָת גִּדְע֥וֹן בֶּן־יוֹאָ֖שׁ בְּשֵׂיבָ֣ה טוֹבָ֑ה וַיִּקָּבֵ֗ר בְּקֶ֨בֶר֙ יוֹאָ֣שׁ אָבִ֔יו בְּעָפְרָ֖ה אֲבִ֥י הָֽעֶזְרִֽי׃פ
records.gloss: And died Gideon son of Joash in old age good, and he was buried in [the] tomb of Joash his father, in Ophrah of [the] Abiezrite[s].
pieces: Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in his father Joash's tomb at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

L.32: And Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age, and he was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

R.32: Gideon son of Joash lived a long, full life and died very old. He was buried in his father Joash's tomb in Ophrah, the town of the Abiezrite clan.

decisions.choice: a good old age: a long life ending in peace
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of Abraham and David (Genesis 15:15; 25:8; 1 Chronicles 29:28): a full life and a peaceful death.

decisions.choice: Ophrah of the Abiezrites: Gideon's home town
decisions.reason: The clan name marks this Ophrah off from the Ophrah in Benjamin (Joshua 18:23). Gideon's family lived there (6:11, 24).

decisions.choice: lived a long, full life and died very old
decisions.reason: Readable says in plain words what "a good old age" means.

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י כַּֽאֲשֶׁר֙ מֵ֣ת גִּדְע֔וֹן וַיָּשׁ֨וּבוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיִּזְנ֖וּ אַחֲרֵ֣י הַבְּעָלִ֑ים וַיָּשִׂ֧ימוּ לָהֶ֛ם בַּ֥עַל בְּרִ֖ית לֵאלֹהִֽים׃
records.gloss: And it was, as had died Gideon, and turned back [the] sons of Israel and prostituted themselves after the Baals, and they set for themselves Baal-berith as god.
pieces: As soon as Gideon was dead, the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} turned away again and prostituted themselves to the Baals. They made Baal-berith their god.

L.33: And it was, when Gideon had died, that the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel turned back and prostituted themselves after the Baals, and they set up Baal-berith for themselves as god.

R.33: As soon as Gideon died, the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} turned away from God again. They were unfaithful to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and worshiped the Baals, and they made Baal-berith their god.

decisions.choice: when the judge died, Israel turned back
decisions.reason: The book's pattern: after each judge died, the people turned away again (2:19).

decisions.choice: Baal-berith: "Baal of the covenant", the god of Shechem
decisions.reason: His temple stood in Shechem, and its silver paid for Abimelech's men (9:4, 46). The name may mean a god who guarded treaties, a bitter name given Israel's covenant with the LORD.

decisions.choice: prostituted themselves: as in verse 27
decisions.reason: Worshiping the Baals is pictured as unfaithfulness in marriage.

decisions.choice: the Baals: the local forms of the god Baal
decisions.reason: Baal was worshiped under many local names and in many shrines, so the plural is used (2:11).

decisions.choice: turned away from God; unfaithful to him
decisions.reason: Readable says from whom they turned and what the picture of prostitution means, as in verse 27.

records.source: וְלֹ֤א זָֽכְרוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵיהֶ֑ם הַמַּצִּ֥יל אוֹתָ֛ם מִיַּ֥ד כָּל־אֹיְבֵיהֶ֖ם מִסָּבִֽיב׃
records.gloss: And not remembered [the] sons of Israel Yahweh their God, who delivered them from [the] hand of all their enemies from all around.
pieces: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did not remember {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God, who had rescued them from the power of all the enemies around them.

L.34: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel did not remember {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies all around.

R.34: The {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} forgot about {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God, who had rescued them from all the enemies around them.

decisions.choice: did not remember: did not stay loyal to
decisions.reason: To remember the LORD is to keep him in mind and live by it (Deuteronomy 8:18); not to remember him is to turn from him, which Moses warned against (Deuteronomy 8:11-14).

decisions.choice: the hand of their enemies: their enemies' power
decisions.reason: As in verse 22.

decisions.choice: forgot about
decisions.reason: Readable says "forgot", the plain opposite of "remember".

records.source: וְלֹֽא־עָשׂ֣וּ חֶ֔סֶד עִם־בֵּ֥ית יְרֻבַּ֖עַל גִּדְע֑וֹן כְּכָל־הַטּוֹבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה עִם־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ
records.gloss: And not they did loyal love with [the] house of Jerubbaal, Gideon, according to all the good which he had done with Israel.
pieces: Nor did they show faithful love to the family of Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, in return for all the good he had done for Israel.

L.35: And they did not do steadfast love with the house of Jerubbaal, Gideon, according to all the good that he had done with Israel.

R.35: They did not show faithful love to the family of Gideon, who was also called Jerubbaal, even though he had done so much good for Israel.

decisions.choice: steadfast love: the faithfulness owed in return for kindness
decisions.reason: The word means steady, faithful kindness that keeps a bond (Ruth 1:8; Joshua 2:12). Gideon had done Israel great good, and they owed his family loyalty in return.

decisions.choice: the house of Jerubbaal: Gideon's sons
decisions.reason: The next chapter shows what this failure meant: Shechem backed Abimelech when he killed Gideon's sons, and Jotham charges them with not treating Jerubbaal's house well (9:5, 16-19).

decisions.choice: Jerubbaal, Gideon: the two names side by side
decisions.reason: Both names are given, linking this chapter to the next, which uses "Jerubbaal" (9:1-2).

decisions.choice: steadfast love (L); faithful love (B, R); family
decisions.reason: Literal says "steadfast love" and Balanced and Readable "faithful love", as in 1:24, Exodus 34:6 and Deuteronomy. Balanced and Readable say "family" for "house".
